q: "The purpose of visualization is insight, not pictures." Who said it?
e: Tukey: 'The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.'

q: "The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see." Who said it?
e: Anscombe: 'A computer should make both calculations and graphs.'

q: Which is NOT one of the four visualization goals listed in lecture?
e: The four goals: record information, analyze data to support reasoning, confirm hypotheses, and communicate ideas to others.

q: John Snow's 1854 map of the London cholera outbreak is the lecture's example of which goal?
e: Nightingale (1856) and Minard (1861) are the examples for communicating ideas.

q: Florence Nightingale (1856) and Joseph Minard (1861) are examples of visualization used to:
e: Minard's chart shows Napoleon's march on Moscow.

q: Why does visualization work, according to the lecture?
a: Cognition and memory are limited; visualization uses perception and pictures to enhance working memory
e: Examples: the 'find the most common number' and multiplication exercises. But visualization can also deceive you.

q: Approximately how many rods and cones does the human eye have?
a: About 120 million rods and 5–6 million cones
w: About 5 million rods and 120 million cones
e: Cones handle color. Rods handle low light.

q: Saccadic eye movements are:
a: Rapid involuntary eye movements (20–100 ms), between fixations of 200–600 ms
e: Our vision at any moment is limited, and the brain 'fills in the missing pieces'.

q: Takeaway from foveation, saccades and the blind spot:
a: Be careful placing too much data on the screen; crisp, clear visualizations work best
w: Use as much data as possible
e: Our high-acuity vision covers only a small area at a time.

q: The Hermann grid, Cornsweet illusion and Mach banding show that our visual system:
a: Is attracted to edges and sensitive to differences, not absolute values
e: Takeaway: maximize contrast with the background if shape outlines matter.

q: Weber's Law says we judge based on:
e: That's why an axis of alignment or reference lines help comparisons.

q: The checker-shadow illusion (same gray looks different in shadow) demonstrates:
a: Simultaneous contrast: judgments are relative to local context
e: Takeaway: don't place data in difficult contexts. Choose position and orientation carefully.

q: Pre-attentive processing (popout) is:
a: Very fast (<200 ms), and what matters most is contrast between features
e: Despite the name, it still requires some attention.

q: Why use a single channel at a time to make a target pop out?
a: Conjunctions of features (e.g., red AND circle) don't pop out; they require serial search
e: Use color and shape sparingly to make the important information pop out.

q: The Gestalt principle that things visually close together are perceived as related is:
e: Similarity is about looking alike (size, color, shape).

q: We see incomplete shapes as complete. Which Gestalt principle?
e: Continuity: we complete hidden objects into simple, familiar shapes.

q: Elements moving in the same direction are perceived as a unit. Which Gestalt principle?
e: 'Gestalt' is German for 'form'. Patterns transcend the stimuli that produced them.

q: Which Gestalt grouping principle is the lecture's example of the strongest cue (lines between dots)?
e: Grouping cues: similarity, connection, enclosure, proximity. Poor use can make viewers see things that aren't there.

q: Color is NOT simply wavelength; it is:
a: A combination of wavelengths and energy, interpreted by our cones
e: The CIE color space comes from 1920s–30s experiments showing humans can match any visible light with three primaries.

q: Additive color (light) uses primaries ___; subtractive color (print ink) uses primaries ___.
a: RGB; CMY (plus K for true black)
e: Approximate black = C+M+Y. True black uses K. Both are device-dependent.

q: A drawback of the RGB color space:
a: It's not perceptually uniform (and actual color is device-dependent)
e: HSV is a polar representation of RGB that's more intuitive for tuning.

q: In HSV, saturation corresponds to:
a: The amount of white mixed in
w: The amount of black mixed in
e: Hue is 'the color'. Luminance/value is the amount of black mixed in.

q: CIE LAB is:
a: A perceptually based space: L* = lightness, a = red–green, b = yellow–blue
e: It's mathematically defined to include all perceivable colors.

q: Roughly how common is color deficiency among people of European descent?
a: 5–8% of men and about 0.5% of women
e: The photopigment genes are on the X chromosome.

q: Deuteranopia is:
e: Protanopia = no red, tritanopia = no blue. Monochromacy = 1-D color vision (very rare).

q: The most common form of color deficiency is:
a: Deuteranomaly (shift in green; poor red–green discrimination)
e: Anomalous trichromacy means one cone is shifted in sensitivity (impairment rather than loss).

q: We have higher contrast sensitivity in which channel, so it's preferred for encoding detail?
e: 'Get it right in black and white.' (Maureen Stone)

q: Minimum and ideal luminance contrast ratios for text:
e: Color is relative, so put ordinal color encodings on a solid, neutral background.

q: Bertin: 'the smaller the mark, ___'.
a: The less distinguishable are the colors
w: The more colors you can use
e: Use bright, saturated colors in small regions and low-saturation pastels for large regions and backgrounds.

q: How many simultaneous colors can people reliably distinguish (for categories)?
e: Categorical colors are easier to remember if they're nameable.

q: For ORDINAL data, which color properties work best?
a: Luminance and saturation (they have an inherent ordering)
e: Hue is great for categorical data because it has no inherent ordering.

q: Which is a known problem with rainbow colormaps?
a: Uneven perceived contrast and no explicit zero crossing
e: See Borland 2007. Rainbows create artificial bands and hide structure.

q: Bivariate colormaps are difficult to interpret unless:
a: At least one of the variables is binary
e: Colormap types: categorical vs. ordered, sequential vs. diverging, segmented vs. continuous, univariate vs. bivariate.

q: Which color harmony uses hues often found in nature that are harmonious and pleasing?
e: Complementary = high contrast. Split-complementary = strong contrast with less tension.

q: Which tool is listed for choosing colormaps for maps and charts?
e: Others: paletton.com, Vischeck (colorblind simulation), Color Buddy.

q: The what-why-how framework asks:
a: What is shown (data), why the user is looking (task), how it's shown (encoding/interaction)
w: Who made it, when, and where
What it costs, why it's slow, how to speed it up
What color, which font, how large
e: Its abstract vocabulary avoids domain-specific terms.

q: The five basic data types are:
e: These combine into dataset types such as tables, networks/trees, and fields.

q: In a table dataset, each row is an ___ and each column is an ___.
e: A cell holds the value for one item and one attribute.

q: Networks and trees consist of:
e: Fields have grids, positions and attributes. Tables have items and attributes.

q: Field attributes at each cell can be scalar, vector, or:
e: Scalar = one value, vector = direction + magnitude, tensor = an array of values.

q: Which grid type is listed?
e: Grid choices affect how continuous data is interpreted.

q: The two key considerations for continuous field data are:
a: Sampling (where attributes are measured) and interpolation (modeling values in between)
e: Grid choices (uniform, rectilinear, structured, unstructured) affect both.

q: Attributes with a meaningful magnitude, where arithmetic makes sense, are:
e: Categorical (nominal) attributes have no implicit ordering. Ordinal ones are ordered without meaningful magnitude.

q: T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL) are an example of which attribute type?
e: They're ordered, but you can't meaningfully subtract them.

q: Ordered attributes can further be:
e: Diverging data has a meaningful midpoint (e.g., 0). Cyclic data wraps around (e.g., days of the week).

q: Turning temperatures (−32.52, 54.06...) into 'hot, warm, cold' creates:
a: A derived attribute (quantitative → ordinal), using the conceptual model
e: The data model is a mathematical abstraction. The conceptual model adds semantics and motivates abstraction choices.

q: 'Above freezing / below freezing' as a derived attribute is what type?
e: Same data, different abstractions: quantitative, ordinal (hot/warm/cold), categorical (above/below freezing).

q: Marks are graphical elements classified by number of spatial dimensions. Which list is correct?
e: Marks can represent items (nodes) or links (via containment or connection).

q: Channels are:
a: Parameters that control the appearance of marks (position, color, size, shape...)
e: Identity channels tell 'what or where'. Magnitude channels tell 'how much'.

q: Which channel type is shape?
e: Size and tilt are magnitude channels. Position and color can serve as both.

q: The expressiveness principle says:
a: Match channel type to attribute type: magnitude channels for ordered data, identity channels for categorical
w: Use as many channels as possible
e: The effectiveness principle says to encode the most important attributes with the most effective channels.

q: The MOST effective magnitude channel for ordered attributes is:
e: Then position on an unaligned scale, length, tilt, area, depth, luminance/saturation, curvature, and volume.

q: The LEAST effective magnitude channels in the ranking are:
e: Area beats volume. Luminance and saturation are ranked about the same.

q: The most effective identity channel for categorical attributes is:
e: Order: spatial region, color hue, motion, shape.

q: Cleveland & McGill (1985) and Heer & Bostock (2010, Mechanical Turk) are sources of:
e: Bertin (1967) and Mackinlay (1986) also contributed.

q: Separable vs. integral channels: which pair is INTEGRAL (perceived holistically)?
e: Pairs run from separable (color/location) toward integral (x-size/y-size, red-green/yellow-blue).

q: Discriminability asks:
a: Can differences in a channel actually be discerned?
e: There's a limit to how many distinct steps a channel can show.

q: Why is 3D generally a poor choice for encoding data?
a: We see the world in 2.5D; perspective interferes with size/color, causes occlusion, and hurts text legibility
e: The power of planar position doesn't extend to 3D depth.

q: Animation is GOOD for which use?
w: Comparing complex state changes over time
Showing multiple states with multiple changes
e: For multiple states with multiple changes, use small multiples instead.

q: Why are small multiples better than animation for comparing many states?
a: Comparing views by moving your eyes (external memory) is easier than comparing to memory of what you saw
e: Visualization works partly by enhancing working memory.

q: Tufte's graphical excellence: give the viewer the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time with:
a: The least ink in the smallest space
e: Einstein: 'An explanation should be as simple as possible, but no simpler.'

q: Tufte's Lie Factor equals:
a: Size of effect shown in graphic ÷ size of effect in data
e: Ideally it's 1.

q: Tufte's integrity principle: the representation of numbers as physically measured on the graphic should be:
a: Directly proportional to the numerical quantities represented
e: Also: show data variation, not design variation.

q: When scaling circles by DIAMETER instead of area, the visual effect is:
a: Exaggerated, because area grows with the square of the diameter
e: Unintended size coding is a common distortion (e.g., pictogram bars).

q: When is truncating the y-axis (non-zero baseline) acceptable, per lecture?
a: When zero doesn't make sense, to emphasize relative position, or when it's the norm (e.g., stock charts)
e: Missing scales and missing baselines can mislead badly.

q: Which is NOT one of the listed options for handling outliers?
a: Delete them from the dataset silently
e: The three options are clipping, scale breaks, and log scales.

q: Data-ink ratio = ?
a: Data-ink ÷ total ink used in the graphic
e: Tufte says to maximize it. A counterpoint EEG study found the most minimal box plot was the hardest to interpret.

q: Bateman et al. (CHI 2010) found that embellished 'chart junk' charts, compared to plain ones:
a: Had similar accuracy, but significantly better long-term recall (2–3 weeks)
e: Viewers also saw value messages more often and enjoyed them more (e.g., Nigel Holmes' TIME graphics).

q: Borkin et al.'s 'What Makes a Visualization Memorable?' found that:
a: Color and human-recognizable objects enhance memorability; common graphs are less memorable than unique types
e: Observers were consistent about which visualizations they remembered. Verdict on chart junk: it depends.

q: Data density = ?
a: Number of entries in the data array ÷ area of the data graphic
e: Maximize it by shrinking graphics: small multiples and sparklines.

q: Trellis plots subdivide space for comparison across plots, typically using which variables as subdivision dimensions?
e: They're a form of small multiples.

q: 'Overestimate of breadth' in illusions of visual bandwidth means designers believe:
a: Viewers can take in all (or most) of the details of a scene at once
w: Viewers attend to every region of the display
Attending to an object gives deep understanding
e: 'Countenance' is the overestimate of how much of the display users attend to. 'Depth' is the overestimate of how deep their understanding goes.

q: The 3D Apple smartphone-share pie chart (Steve Jobs keynote) misled because:
a: 3D perspective made Apple's 19.5% slice look larger than RIM's 21.2%
e: A plain bar chart sorted by value shows the true ranking.

q: Why are dual-axis charts risky (e.g., the 2015 Planned Parenthood chart)?
a: Independent scales can make lines cross or diverge arbitrarily, implying false relationships
e: That chart also lacked an axis and context ('insufficient context', Alberto Cairo's How Charts Lie).

q: In Munzner's framework, tasks are abstracted as:
a: {action, target} pairs (e.g., discover distribution, compare trends, locate outliers)
e: Actions describe why. Targets describe what in the data.

q: Under 'Analyze → Consume', the three goals are:
e: 'Produce' includes annotate, record, and derive.

q: Search when you know the target but NOT its location is called:
e: Lookup = target and location known. Browse = location known, target unknown. Explore = both unknown.

q: Search when neither the target nor its location is known:
e: Query actions: identify (one), compare (some), summarize (all).

q: Query actions scale from one target to all targets as:
e: These are the 'how many targets' levels of a query.

q: Targets for 'all data' include:
e: Attribute targets: distribution and extremes (one), dependency/correlation/similarity (many). Network: topology and paths. Spatial: shape.

q: Amar et al.'s low-level task 'Find Extremum' is:
a: Find data cases with an extreme value of an attribute (e.g., car with the highest MPG)
w: Rank cases by an ordinal metric
e: Amar et al. (InfoVis 2005) list 10 tasks: retrieve value, filter, compute derived value, find extremum, sort, determine range, characterize distribution, find anomalies, cluster, correlate.

q: 'What is the average calorie content of Post cereals?' is which Amar et al. task?
e: It computes an aggregate over a set of cases.

q: 'Are there any outliers in protein?' is which Amar et al. task?
e: It identifies cases unexpected relative to a relationship or expectation.

q: 'Which Kellogg's cereals have high fiber?' is which Amar et al. task?
e: It finds data cases satisfying concrete conditions.

q: Which is NOT one of the interaction types listed in lecture?
e: The list: change over time, rearranging, selection & highlighting, linking, filtering, navigation.

q: Geometric vs. semantic zooming:
a: Geometric just magnifies; semantic changes what is shown (level of detail) as you zoom
e: For example, a map that reveals street names only when zoomed in is semantic zooming.

q: Crossfilter (Square) is the lecture's example of which interaction?
e: Linking is shown with GeogTreeMaps, and selection with the NYT movie revenue graphic.
